question: What is the main reason we use patient isolation in the hospital?

options.A: To reduce the overall cost of hospital supplies
options.B: To punish patients who refuse to take their prescribed medication
options.C: To stop germs from spreading to other patients and staff
options.D: To give the patient a quiet room for undisturbed rest

explanation: You got this! Isolation acts as a shield to keep infectious bugs contained so that everyone else on the ward stays safe and healthy.

question: At which point in the chain of infection does patient isolation work best?
explanation: Brilliant! By keeping an infected patient apart and limiting contact, isolation blocks the exact pathway germs use to travel from person to person.

question: Which type of precautions must you use for every single patient, no matter their diagnosis?
explanation: Spot on! Standard Precautions are our trusty baseline defense for every patient encounter because we never know an infection's status right away.

question: A patient with an undiagnosed chronic cough is admitted to your ward. What precautions should you use first?

options.D: No precautions until lab results return

explanation: Well done! Always start with Standard Precautions for every new admission until specific lab results or doctor's orders guide you otherwise.

question: Which type of precautions calls for wearing a specially fitted N95 respirator mask?
explanation: You nailed it! Airborne bugs float around on tiny particles, so we need that high-level N95 protection to keep our lungs safe.

question: Why do droplet precautions only need a regular surgical mask instead of an N95?

options.A: Droplets are heavy, travel short distances, and do not linger in the air
options.B: Droplets evaporate instantly before reaching any healthcare worker
options.C: Droplets can only pass through skin pores, not through cloth
options.D: Surgical masks filter out microscopic floating particles better than N95s

explanation: Exactly! Large droplets quickly drop down rather than floating, so a simple surgical mask gives you all the protection you need for close care.

question: When entering an isolation room, what is the very first piece of PPE you should put on?
explanation: Great job! Think of it from the body up: you put your gown on first to cover your uniform completely before touching masks or gloves.

question: Why must you take off your gloves before removing your isolation gown during doffing?

options.A: To make it easier to tie the gown strings behind your back for the next shift
options.B: To prevent contaminating your hands and clothing with germs on the outside of the gown
options.C: To ensure the gown remains sterile for the next healthcare worker
options.D: To save time while exiting the patient care area in a busy ward

explanation: You're doing great! Your gloves carry the most germs, so taking them off first stops you from accidentally spreading pathogens to your clean hands and uniform.

question: What type of room air pressure is needed for a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis?
explanation: Spot on! Negative pressure acts like a trap, making sure air rushes inside when the door opens instead of leaking out into the hallway.

question: Why do we use a positive pressure room for an immunocompromised patient?

options.A: To make it easier for nurses to administer intravenous fluids quickly
options.B: To keep the room temperature warm enough for a patient with a fever
options.C: To blow contaminated air away from the patient so outside particles cannot enter
options.D: To suck all germs out of the patient's bloodstream through the ventilation vents

explanation: Wonderful! Positive pressure pushes clean air outward, acting as an invisible shield to protect a vulnerable patient from outside dust and germs.

question: What is a common emotional challenge faced by patients stuck in long-term isolation?

options.B: A sudden increase in physical stamina

explanation: That's right. Being cut off from loved ones and normal human contact can feel really heavy, so our emotional support matters just as much as medical care!

question: A patient in contact isolation feels depressed and refuses to open their door for nursing care. What is your best action as a nurse?

options.A: Remove the isolation sign so family members can crowd into the room
options.B: Threaten to discharge the patient immediately if they do not cooperate with rules
options.C: Acknowledge their feelings, explain the care plan patiently, and spend extra social time with them
options.D: Leave the food tray outside and refuse to enter the room for the rest of the shift

explanation: You've got a true nursing heart! Validating their feelings and showing extra care helps ease their anxiety while keeping safety standards strong.
